ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text: A pond has two populations, zooplankton and algae, and the trends in their population densities over time are shown in the figure. If a large number of a certain kind of fish (C) that specializes in eating zooplankton are released into the pond, after a period of time, only one population remains among the three populations A, B, and C in the pond. What relationships exist between C and B?
ready1_open_rewrite.raw_answer_text: There is both a competitive relationship and a predation relationship

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: First describe the image: In the figure, the vertical axis is labeled "population density", and the horizontal axis is labeled "time". A corresponds to the solid line, and B corresponds to the dashed line. The solid line A and dashed line B both show periodic fluctuations, and in each round of fluctuation, the peak of A appears first, and the peak of B appears later. Then reason: In a predator-prey relationship, the number of prey usually increases first and reaches a peak first, and the predator then increases and reaches a peak. The original pond contains algae and zooplankton, and zooplankton feed on algae, so A, which reaches the peak first, should be algae, and B, which reaches the peak later, should be zooplankton. The stem says that C is a fish that specializes in eating zooplankton, so C preys on B. At the same time, C and B live in the same pond and will compete for certain resources such as living space and oxygen, and the stem states that after a period of time only one population remains among A, B, and C, reflecting interspecific exclusion, so there is also a competitive relationship between C and B.
